title: Same hill, new neighbours
place: Fields on Llandough hill, above the River Ely

cast.A_MARY: a Romano-British farm woman, his wife (prologue, invented)

shots.direction: About 4 s. Date-and-place card over a wide establishing still (same hill and viewpoint as scene 2, roundhouses gone). Late summer; half the field reaped spelt stubble, half standing grain; a small wattle-and-thatch barn; thin smoke beyond the crest. Slow push-in. Ambience: wind in the grain, skylarks, distant geese.

shots.direction: About 14 s. Medium close-up on the farmer. He straightens, rubs a spelt ear between his palms and blows off the chaff. He glances up at the smoke over the brow, then speaks to his wife.

lines.accent: South Wales (Glamorgan) Welsh, rural; native review
lines.cy: Weli di'r mwg dros y grib? Ma' tân 'da nhw lan yn y tŷ cerrig yn barod. Sbelt da eleni. Digon sych i'w ddyrnu cyn i'r glaw ddod lan y cwm.
lines.en: See the smoke over the brow? They've the fires lit up at the stone house already. Good spelt this year. Dry enough to thresh before the rain comes up the valley.
lines.es: ¿Ves el humo sobre la cresta? Ya prendieron los fuegos allá arriba en la casa de piedra. Buen trigo espelta este año. Bastante seco para trillarlo antes de que la lluvia suba por el valle.

shots.direction: About 14 s. Medium close-up on the wife, who keeps binding the sheaf as she answers. She tilts her head towards a basket where a red glossy bowl sits among bread and cheese.
shots.image_prompt: Photoreal 16:9 cinematic medium close-up, Roman-period Britain c. AD 200. Beside her a wicker basket holds a glossy red pottery bowl, bread and a cloth. Hillside harvest field, warm late-summer light. Invented face, no text, no heraldry.

lines.accent: South Wales (Glamorgan) Welsh, rural; native review
lines.cy: Dyrna fe'n glou, 'te. Ma'r freuan yn llwgu, a'r plant 'fyd. Potiau coch crand o bell, a ni'n dal i fyta'r un uwd mas ohonyn nhw.
lines.en: Then thresh it quick. The quern's hungry, and so are the children. Fine red pots from far off, and we still eat the same porridge out of them.
lines.es: Entonces trillalo rápido. La piedra de moler tiene hambre, y los chicos también. Ollas rojas finas de lejos, y seguimos comiendo la misma mazamorra en ellas.

shots.direction: About 10 s. Medium still with a slow lateral move. The farmer cuts spelt with an iron sickle. Behind him his wife binds a sheaf with a twist of straw. Hands, straw and dust are lit by the sun. Over the brow of the hill, out of frame, a thin thread of chimney smoke rises from the stone house; the house itself is never shown. Ambience only. Placed after the first exchange so its PX-02 caption appears after 0:30.

shots.direction: About 12 s. Medium shot of the farmer leaning on the sickle. He looks across to the wattle barn and the yoked oxen beside it, where the old roundhouse of the previous scene once stood.

Inland hillside, marshland and river far below. Golden afternoon light. Invented face, no text, no heraldry.

lines.accent: South Wales (Glamorgan) Welsh, rural; native review
lines.cy: Ro'dd Mam-gu'n arfer gweud bod ei phobol hi'n cadw tŷ crwn fan hyn. Nawr, y sgubor a'r ychen sy 'ma.
lines.en: Gran used to tell us her people kept a round house right here. Now it's the barn and the oxen.
lines.es: La abuela contaba que su gente tenía una casa redonda justo acá. Ahora es el granero y los bueyes.

shots.direction: About 9 s. Ambient still, slow push-in: geese walk between the stooks; the barn, the yoked oxen and the cart behind; grey cloud rising off the marshes below. Ambience: geese, a lowing ox, wind.
shots.image_prompt: Same hill and viewpoint, about AD 200, late afternoon: closer view of the reaped stubble near the field edge, plump white and grey geese walking between stooked spelt sheaves, a small wattle-and-thatch barn with two yoked oxen and a wooden cart behind them. Remove all roundhouses. Grey cloud starting to rise off the marshes far below. No people.

shots.direction: About 18 s. Medium close-up on the wife. She looks down the slope, where grey cloud is rising off the marshes of the Ely. A gaggle of fat geese waddles along the stubble behind her, and she half-smiles at them.

Plump white and grey geese walk across the stubble behind her. Inland landscape, no sea. Changing light, the first shadows of cloud. Invented face, no text, no heraldry.

lines.accent: South Wales (Glamorgan) Welsh, rural; native review
lines.cy: Galw nhw miwn, 'te. Ma' cwmwl yn dod lan o'r gors. A ma'r gwyddau'n dew eleni: un at droad y flwyddyn, ac un i dy fam, neu chlywn ni byth diwedd y peth.
lines.en: Call them in, then. There's cloud coming up off the marsh. And the geese are fat this year: one for the turn of the year, and one for your mother, or we'll never hear the end of it.
lines.es: Llamalos, entonces. Viene una nube subiendo del bañado. Y los gansos están gordos este año: uno para el cambio de año, y otro para tu mamá, o no nos lo va a perdonar nunca.

shots.direction: About 8 s. Close shot of the farmer laughing. He waves the geese off the sheaves with a wave of his hand rather than chasing them.
shots.image_prompt: Photoreal 16:9 cinematic close shot, Roman-period Britain c. AD 200. A weathered farmer in his fifties with a broad face, grey-flecked beard and heavy hands laughs warmly and waves a hand at geese wandering past stooked spelt sheaves. Coarse wool tunic and cloak, bareheaded. Hillside field, soft overcast light arriving. Invented face, no text, no heraldry.

lines.accent: South Wales (Glamorgan) Welsh, rural; native review
lines.cy: Gad iddyn nhw redeg. Ma'r bryn yn ddigon mawr i bob un ohonon ni.
lines.en: Let them run. The hill's big enough for all of us.
lines.es: Dejalos correr. La loma es bastante grande para todos nosotros.

shots.direction: About 12 s. Wide closing still with a slow pull-back. The ox cart, loaded with sheaves, creaks up the track towards the brow with the couple walking beside it. The smoke from beyond the crest drifts in the wind; the stone house stays out of frame. Cloud rolls up over the marshes and the river below. Ambience: cart wheels, oxen, geese, the first drops of rain.

continuity: The rain comes up the valley over the cart track; on the same slope, centuries later, the next scene finds a monk of Llandough leading a burial in the monastic cemetery above the marshes of the Ely.
